## The strategic reality first

The headline from GitHub Universe 2025 is **Agent HQ / Mission Control** — "orchestrate any agent, any way you work," with agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cognition, and xAI running *inside* GitHub, assigned in parallel, monitored from web/VS Code/mobile/CLI. That is **almost exactly Entire's thesis** (an agent-agnostic control plane over Claude Code, Gemini, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Droid, OpenCode, Pi).

So two things are true at once: GitHub just validated your bet, and it's now walking onto your lawn. "Beating GitHub" is less about matching feature-for-feature and more about being **loud where GitHub structurally can't follow**: local-first, not-locked-to-GitHub, step-level rewind, and prompt-level provenance. Details below.

## Feature-by-feature map

| GitHub AI feature (2025–26) | What Entire has today | Gap / opportunity |
|---|---|---|
| **Mission Control** — live command center, parallel agents, monitor from any device | `activity`, `dispatch`, `session list` — *retrospective* views | **Biggest gap.** No live orchestration surface to launch/watch/steer multiple agents running *now* |
| **Coding agent** — issue → branch → draft PR, async in Actions, live session logs | `investigate --issue-link` (findings/fixes), `dispatch` (summaries) | Partial. No true "assign issue → agent works on a branch → opens PR" loop |
| **Agentic code review** — full-repo context, inline PR comments, self-review before PR, auto-fix | `entire review` — multi-agent + judge, posts to *trails* | Doesn't post **GitHub PR inline comments**; no findings→fixer feedback loop |
| **Security in the agent workflow** — secret/code/dep scanning of the *produced diff* before PR | Secret scanning of **transcripts** (OPF redaction before cloud) | Different axis. You redact what you *store*; you don't scan the *code the agent wrote* for leaked keys / vuln deps |
| **Copilot Spaces** — persistent context containers grounding future work | Transcripts + `search` + `why`/`blame` | You have *richer* raw material (actual reasoning) but no curated "grounding space" that auto-feeds new sessions |
| **Custom agents / AGENTS.md** — source-controlled personas w/ prompts+tools | Review profiles (`agents`, `skills`) | Personas exist only inside `review`; not a first-class cross-command concept |
| **Plan Mode** — clarifying Qs before implementing | — | Minor; more an agent-harness feature than control-plane |
| **MCP Registry** — discover/install MCP tools | `plugin` + `mcp` stdio server | Partial; no registry/marketplace |
| **Copilot Metrics Dashboard** — org adoption/impact/cost | `tokens profile`, `activity`, control-plane `org/project` | You have the data (tokens, checkpoints); no aggregated org dashboard |
| **Enterprise governance** — locked-down agent tokens, audit logs, policy | `org/project/repo/grant` control-plane | Partial; no explicit agent permission/policy + audit layer |

## Where you already win (lean in, don't rebuild)

- **Step-level checkpoints + rewind** — GitHub is commit/PR-granular; you're per-agent-step. Nobody else can rewind mid-session.
- **Prompt-level provenance** — `why`/`blame`/attribution ties every *line → prompt → session → decision*. Agent HQ has none of this.
- **Local-first + truly agent-agnostic** — works with 8 agents and without a GitHub remote. GitHub's control plane only orchestrates agents GitHub blesses, inside GitHub.
- **Privacy filter (OPF)** — a real enterprise wedge for shops nervous about shipping transcripts to a cloud.

1. **Live "Mission Control" TUI** *(highest leverage — directly answers Agent HQ)*. Launch/watch/steer N parallel agent sessions with live status, token burn, and one-key rewind. You already record sessions; add the live layer. Your differentiator vs GitHub: **rewind any agent to any step live.**

4. **Diff-level security scan.** Scan the agent's *produced changes* for leaked secrets and vulnerable deps at checkpoint/pre-push — complementary to your transcript redaction, closing the one place GitHub is clearly ahead.
5. **"Team memory" grounding (beat Copilot Spaces).** Turn transcripts + `why`/`search` into curated context that auto-grounds new sessions. Spaces ground on docs; you can ground on *what the team actually decided and why.*
6. **Org analytics dashboard.** Aggregate the token/checkpoint/activity data you already collect into adoption/impact/cost per team/agent — cheap to build, strong for enterprise sales.
7. **Agent guardrails + audit policy.** Formalize `grant`/control-plane into per-agent permissions + audit log (governance parity).

Understand how to mirror existing GitHub repositories on Entire.

Repo mirrors let you bring existing GitHub repositories into Entire’s AI-native development workflows, where agents, automation, and humans work with the same Git repositories.
A mirror exposes an existing GitHub repo as an Entire-backed Git remote. You use it through an entire:// URL, so standard Git commands like clone, fetch, pull, and push can talk to Entire without changing your Git tooling.
This makes mirrors a low-friction way to try Entire on real code, connect agents or automation to an Entire-backed Git remote, and evaluate Entire in an existing workflow before changing how the broader team works.
​
Why Use a Mirror?
Use a repo mirror when you want to:
Try Entire’s AI-native development workflows on an existing project, rather than creating a throwaway repo that does not reflect how your team actually works.
Give agents or scripts an Entire-backed Git remote for code that already lives in GitHub.
Evaluate Entire in a real workflow without coordinating a team-wide Git remote change. You can start with one checkout, agent, or script.
Use Entire for clone, fetch, and push workflows while keeping your current GitHub repository and permissions model in place.
​
Common Actions
With a repo mirror, you can:
Create a mirror for an existing GitHub repository.
Clone the mirror with an entire:// URL.
Set an existing local checkout’s Git remote to the mirror URL.
Push through the mirror to the upstream GitHub repository.
Restore the original GitHub remote URL if you need to switch back.
Remove a mirror when you no longer need it.
For command syntax and flags, see the CLI command reference.
​
What to Expect
Creating a mirror does not delete, move, or rewrite the GitHub repository.
Changing a local checkout’s remote only updates that checkout’s .git/config. It does not create or delete the server-side mirror.
Removing a mirror does not change local Git remotes that you already configured.

Mirror an existing GitHub repository on Entire and use it with Git.

​
Prerequisites
Before you create a mirror, make sure you have:
The Entire CLI installed. The latest version you should have installed is 0.7.3.
You have access to clone the GitHub repository you want to mirror
​
Verify the Mirror Command Is Available
entire repo mirror create --help
If the mirror command is not available, update the Entire CLI to the latest version, 0.7.3.
​
Log In
Log in with the Entire CLI:
entire login
Confirm that your login is active:
entire auth status
​
Check GitHub App Access
Before you create or push through a mirror, confirm that the Entire GitHub App can access the repository.
Open GitHub installed apps.
Find Entire.
If GitHub shows Permission updates requested, click Review request and approve the update.
Click Configure for Entire.
To choose which repositories Entire can access, under Repository access, choose All repositories or Only select repositories, then click Save.
​
Create the Mirror
Choose the GitHub repository you want to mirror.
export GH_OWNER="<owner>"
export GH_REPO="<repo>"
Create the mirror placement:
entire repo mirror create "github.com/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
This registers the mirror on Entire. It does not change any local Git checkout.
The repository can be written as owner/repo, an HTTPS GitHub URL, or an SSH GitHub URL. By default, the command waits until the initial clone is available on Entire.
The command prints the mirror URL when it succeeds:
Registered mirror <mirror-id>
  entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/<owner>/<repo>
  cloning. ready
​
Use the Mirror With Git
To clone the mirror into a new checkout, use the URL printed by entire repo mirror create:
git clone "entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
From an existing clone of the GitHub repository, point the local origin remote at the mirror:
cd "$GH_REPO"
git remote get-url origin
git remote set-url origin "entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
git fetch origin
If you want to verify the mirror before changing the checkout’s primary remote, add it temporarily as another remote:
cd "$GH_REPO"
git remote add entire "entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
git fetch entire
These commands only update your local .git/config. They do not create or delete the server-side mirror placement.
To restore origin to GitHub, set it back to the original GitHub URL:
git remote set-url origin "git@github.com:$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO.git"
​
Verify Git Still Works
Run a normal Git command through the configured remote:
git fetch
git status
At this point, your local checkout is using the Entire mirror for Git operations.
​
Push Through the Mirror
Create a test branch, make a small change, then stage and commit it:
git switch -c mirror-push-test
echo "Mirror test" >> mirror-test.txt
git add mirror-test.txt
git commit -m "Test mirror push"
Push the commit through the mirror:
git push -u origin mirror-push-test
Entire forwards the push through the mirror to the upstream GitHub repository. Your GitHub write access, branch protection rules, and required checks still apply.
​
Remove the Mirror
When you no longer need a mirror, remove the server-side mirror placement:
entire repo mirror remove "github.com/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
This does not delete or rewrite the GitHub repository. It also does not change any local Git remotes you configured in .git/config.
​
Troubleshooting
​
unknown command "repo"
Your entire binary may be older than the mirror commands. Update the Entire CLI using the installation instructions, then try again.
​
403: Write access to repository not granted
If git push reaches the Entire mirror but GitHub rejects the forwarded push, check the Entire GitHub App permissions:
Open GitHub installed apps.
Find Entire.
If GitHub shows Permission updates requested, click Review request and approve the update.
Click Configure for Entire.
To choose which repositories Entire can access, under Repository access, choose All repositories or Only select repositories, then click Save.
Refresh your Entire login:
entire auth logout
entire auth login
Retry the push after logging in again.
​
doesn't look like a cluster, or it is unreachable
Git could not reach Entire while using the entire:// remote helper. Retry the command first:
git clone "entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO"
If it keeps failing, check your network connection and try again.
​
Mirror creation takes a while
The default create command waits for the initial clone to appear on Entire. For large repositories, that can take time. If you only need to register the placement and check back later, use --no-wait.
​
Restore the original GitHub remote
If you pointed origin at a mirror and want to undo it:
git remote set-url origin "git@github.com:$GH_OWNER/$GH_REPO.git"

## 1. **Is the mirror just a passthrough proxy to GitHub, or does Entire store the repo itself?**

**Entire stores the repo itself.** When you run `entire repo mirror create github.com/octocat/hello-world`, the control plane **clones the GitHub repo directly into the cluster** and stores it there. The flow is:
- CLI calls `c.CreateMirror()` (POST /mirrors on control plane) with owner/repo/clusterHost
- Control plane initiates a GitHub→Entire clone (status: "processing")
- The mirror waits until clone completes (status: "ready")
- Subsequent clones come from Entire's cluster, not GitHub

## 2. **What flows through the entire:// remote helper?**

The entire:// remote helper is a **transparent HTTP proxy for git pack protocol traffic**, not a data storage layer. It does NOT inspect or manipulate git objects:
- Parses `entire://<cluster>/gh/<owner>/<repo>`
- Resolves login context → mints repo-scoped tokens
- Routes git smart-HTTP (git-upload-pack, git-receive-pack) through `transport.Proxy`
- The Proxy applies failover on 5xx, manages replica nodes via X-Entire-Replicas header, strips auth on out-of-cluster redirects
- Classifies operations as "push" or "pull" to mint appropriate tokens

**Evidence:** `/Users/mohit/Desktop/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire/main.go:126-156` wires `setAuth` (token exchange) and creates a `transport.Proxy` that runs `githelper.Run()`. The transport (`/Users/mohit/Desktop/cli/internal/remotehelper/transport/proxy.go:1-10`) is explicitly decoupled from auth and "talks to one or more Entire data-plane replicas." githelper.Run delegates to handleConnect/handleStatelessConnect which relay git protocol frames.

## 3. **Does mirroring connect to checkpoint/session/transcript system?**

**No, mirrors are completely decoupled from checkpoints/AI-native features.** There are NO hooks triggered on mirror push, NO checkpoint attachment, NO transcript sync, NO review invocation. The mirror is a pure git storage/routing facility. The checkpoint system has a separate `checkpoint_remote` setting for *pushing checkpoints to a different repo*, not for using a mirror.

**Evidence:** Searching for "mirror" + "checkpoint|transcript|review|session|hook" in `/Users/mohit/Desktop/cli/cmd/entire/cli/` yields zero results connecting them. `repo_mirror.go` defines only CRUD operations on the control plane. ## 4. **What's the server side? (cluster core / entire.io backend)**

**The cluster core is a full git server (stores objects).** It consists of:
- Control plane (coreapi): REST API accepting CreateMirror / ListMirrors / DeleteMirror at POST/DELETE/GET /mirrors
- Data plane: Multiple replica nodes hosting git smart-HTTP endpoints (git-upload-pack, git-receive-pack)
- Replica discovery: Nodes advertise themselves via X-Entire-Replicas header; clients cache via on-disk `nodes.json`

## What mirroring actually is (from the code)

- `entire repo mirror create` tells Entire's **control plane to clone your GitHub repo into its own cluster** and store the full git objects on data-plane replica nodes (`repo_mirror.go:201`). It waits until status flips `processing → ready`.
- `git clone/fetch/push entire://…` goes through a **custom git remote helper** (`cmd/git-remote-entire/main.go`) that mints a repo-scoped token, classifies the op as push/pull, and **transparently proxies the git pack protocol** to those replicas (`transport/proxy.go`), with failover. Pushes get forwarded upstream to GitHub (your branch protection / write access still apply).
- **Critically: it is 100% decoupled from everything AI-native.** No post-receive hooks. No checkpoint, transcript, review, provenance, or search integration. Zero. It's a full distributed git server whose only job today is *store objects and relay bytes*.

So your instinct is exactly right. **Entire built the hard part — a git server sitting in the data path that forwards to GitHub — and attached zero value to it.** As shipped, the mirror is a naked proxy: it adds a hop, a login, and a trust requirement (all your code now lives on their cluster) in exchange for *nothing a developer feels*. Of course it's not enticing.

But that also means the interesting news: **the expensive infrastructure already exists.** The value is latent, not missing.

## The reframe that makes it enticing

The mirror puts Entire at the **chokepoint of every clone/fetch/push** — the single position GitHub monetizes. Every feature idea should answer one question: *what happens when code flows through Entire that can't happen when it flows through GitHub?* Right now the answer is "nothing." Here's what it should be, ranked by leverage-per-effort:

**Tier 1 — do something at the git chokepoint (server-side post-receive hooks, injection surface (a) the code flagged):**

1. **Review-on-push, before it reaches GitHub.** Push to the mirror → Entire runs the multi-agent review you *already built* (`entire review`) server-side → posts findings / gates the forward-to-GitHub. This is the killer app: zero-setup, CI-quality AI review that works for **any agent or human**, not just people using Entire's agents. It reuses existing machinery, just moved server-side. (Make it async/non-blocking so it never stalls a push.)

2. **Whole-repo provenance, server-side.** Entire is the *only* place that holds both the pushed code (mirror) **and** the prompts/sessions that produced it (checkpoints). So it can answer *"which prompt / agent / session wrote this line"* for the entire repo. GitHub blame shows a commit; Entire blame shows the reasoning. This is your actual moat — no one else has both halves.

3. **Semantic index of code + history + reasoning**, exposed to agents over your existing MCP server. "Ask the repo," grounded in decisions, not just code.

**Tier 2 — the UI you're hinting at (this is where "enticing" actually lives):**

A CLI will never pull anyone off github.com. But the repo already sits on Entire's cluster, so a **web surface at entire.io over the mirror** is a read-layer over data you already have, not a from-scratch build. Show the things GitHub structurally *can't*:
- **Session replay** — watch how a change was built, prompt by prompt, with rewind.
- **Provenance view** — click a line → the session/agent/prompt behind it.
- **Agent activity feed** — human vs. agent contributions across the repo.
- **Review inbox** — the push-time reviews from Tier 1.
- **Semantic search** over code + reasoning.

**Tier 3 — the one-line change that unlocks all of it:** the investigation found the mirror and the checkpoint system are decoupled, but there's already a `checkpoint_remote` setting. **Wire `mirror create` to auto-point checkpoint_remote at the mirror**, so pushing through it auto-attaches provenance. That single connection turns two dead assets into one differentiated product.

## My honest recommendation

Don't pitch the mirror as backup — that framing is a dead end. The sequence I'd actually do:

1. **Connect the two systems** (Tier 3) — small, unlocks everything.
2. **Ship review-on-push** (Tier 1.1) — the first feature a developer would *switch their remote for*, and it reuses code you have.
3. **Build the web provenance/replay UI** (Tier 2) — the "beat GitHub" bet, but only after 1–2 prove the data pipeline.

The whole thing rests on one sentence you can put on a landing page: **"Point your remote at Entire and every push gets reviewed by agents and remembers why it exists — then still lands in GitHub."** That's enticing. "It's a backup" isn't.

# Upstream Host & Auth-Context Resolution

How the CLI decides *which host to dial* and *which login (auth context) to
authenticate as* for every upstream call. The goal is one mental model:

> An **auth context** is a login to one **core** (the identity provider /
> login server). Every upstream call resolves to some host. That host either
> **is** a core — use the active context's core directly — or it is a
> **resource server** that advertises which cores it trusts via a
> `/.well-known` blob, so the CLI picks the context whose core is trusted and
> exchanges that context's token for the resource.

There is no separate "auth system" per service. There is one identity model
(`contexts.json`, keyed on `CoreURL`) and a set of resource servers that
accept a core's JWTs.

## The pieces

| Role | Service (prod / staging) | Hit by | Trusted-core discovery |

| **Core** — IdP **and** control-plane API, co-located | `entire-core` (`us.auth.entire.io`) | `org` / `repo` / `project` / `grant`, `auth *`, `login` | none needed — the host *is* the core |
| **Resource: git cluster** | `entire-server` / `entiredb` | `git-remote-entire` (clone/push) | `/.well-known/entire-cluster.json` → `core_urls` |

`contexts.json` (`$ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR/contexts.json`, shared with entiredb's
CLIs) stores each login as `{Name, CoreURL, Handle, KeychainService}` plus a
`CurrentContext` pointer. `CoreURL` is the JWT `iss` — the core that minted the
token. `entire auth use <ctx>` flips `CurrentContext`.

Straight answer: I overstated it. **"entire-server" is a real name — but it's the name this repo's docs/code use for the *service*, not necessarily the *repo* on your git host.** So you finding "git-sync" instead of a repo literally named "entire-server" is expected, not a contradiction.

Here's what *this* repo actually says the backend is (from its own docs + code, `docs/architecture/upstream-host-resolution.md` and grep):

| Service name (in this repo) | Role | What hits it |
|---|---|---|
| **`entire-core`** (`us.auth.entire.io`) | IdP + control-plane API | `auth`, `login`, `org/repo/project/grant`, **`repo mirror create/remove/list`** (POST /mirrors) |
| **`entire-server`** / **`entiredb`** | the **git cluster / data plane** — clones GitHub, stores objects, serves `git-upload-pack`/`git-receive-pack` | `git-remote-entire` (clone/fetch/push) |
| **`entire.io`** | web/data API | `activity`, `search`, `trail`, `dispatch` |

Note it's dual-named — `githelper/connect.go:79` says "against **entire-server**," while the docs table lists it as "**entire-server / entiredb**." So the git data-plane is referred to by *at least two* names inside this one repo. A third name on the actual repo host (like **`git-sync`**) is entirely plausible — a service whose job is "clone GitHub repos and keep them synced + serve git" is a very natural fit for that name.

So: **I can't confirm from here whether `git-sync` is the same thing** — this repo is a pure client and never names the backend's *repo*. But you can confirm it in ~30 seconds by checking whether `git-sync` contains the tells this repo expects its data plane to expose:

- an HTTP endpoint serving **`/.well-known/entire-cluster.json`** (with a `core_urls` field) — this repo's `clusterdiscovery` fetches exactly that
- **`POST /mirrors`**, `GET /mirrors`, `DELETE /mirrors` handlers (the control-plane side — though that might live in `entire-core` instead)
- git smart-HTTP handlers: **`git-upload-pack` / `git-receive-pack` / `info/refs`**
- anything emitting the **`X-Entire-Replicas`** header (this repo's `transport/proxy.go` reads it for failover)

If `git-sync` has the `git-upload-pack`/`git-receive-pack` + `.well-known/entire-cluster.json` bits, that's your data plane (= `entire-server`/`entiredb`), and it's where server-side review-on-push and the code↔provenance join would live. If it only has the sync/clone logic and no git-serving or `/mirrors`, there's probably a *separate* control-plane repo (the `entire-core` piece) too.

# git-sync: Precise Service Classification

## (1) Architecture Type
**Background relay only.** Not a user-facing git server. The tool mirrors refs between two OTHER remotes without creating a local checkout. Users don't push to git-sync; it pulls from source and pushes to target.

## (2) Protocol Endpoints
**Does NOT expose endpoints.** Instead, it *consumes* them:
- Calls `info/refs` on source and target for ref advertisement
- Calls `upload-pack` on source to fetch
- Calls `receive-pack` on target to push
- Uses "smart HTTP directly" but doesn't serve these endpoints itself

## (3) Hooks/Interception/Middleware
**No hooks mentioned.** The docs contain zero references to callbacks, middleware, custom logic execution points, or interception during transfer. It is a one-way batch operation with no extensibility layer for custom logic on receive or during packfile streaming.

## (4) Storage Model
**Streaming + in-memory only (no durable local store).** The tool uses:
- "in-memory `go-git` object store"
- "Relay path" where "pack data streams from source…directly into target…local process holds no object graph"
- Optional materialized fallback for non-relay cases, still in-memory and bounded by `--materialized-max-objects`

## (5) Mirrors/Replicas/Server Features
**Zero mention.** No `/mirrors` API, replica management, or "entire-server" references. It's a CLI tool and Go library for one-shot sync operations, optionally run from cron or CI—"not a daemon."

**Summary:** git-sync is a *stateless relay CLI*, not a server.

Now I can answer definitively — and the answer is a clear "partly." Let me give it to you straight.

## The decisive facts

- **`git-sync` is *not* the server you'd need.** Its README confirms it's a **stateless relay CLI** — it *calls* `upload-pack`/`receive-pack` on other remotes to copy refs between them; it does **not** serve git endpoints, users don't push to it, it has **no on-receive hook or interception point**, and it stores nothing durably. It's the plumbing that copies refs between GitHub and Entire, run from cron/CI. You can't hang a server-side review gate on it.
- **`cli-checkpoints` is just a git data store** (12k commits, sharded dirs) holding checkpoint/provenance artifacts. No API, no server code.
- **The actual product backend you'd need — `entire-core` (control plane + `/mirrors` API), `entire-server`/`entiredb` (the user-facing git data plane), `entire.io` (web/data/search) — is not in your list.**

## So: can you do both versions?

| Version | With only these repos? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **#1 client-side** — `mirror create` auto-wires `checkpoint_remote→mirror` | ✅ **Yes** | `cli` repo, self-contained |
| **#2 client-side** — pre-push hook runs local `entire review` | ✅ **Yes** | `cli` repo, reuses local agent |
| **#2 "central" — review runs in CI whenever git-sync mirrors** | ⚠️ **Yes-ish** | `git-sync` + `cli` + a CI runner + an API key in CI |
| **#1 headline** — backend *joins & serves* code↔provenance (blame/replay) | ❌ **No** | needs `entire-core` + `entire.io` |
| **#2 true server gate** — reviewed on the git server before forwarding | ❌ **No** | needs `entire-server`/`entiredb` |
| **Web UI over the mirror** | ❌ **No** | needs `entire.io` |

## The honest read

**Both *client-side* versions: fully buildable — they're 100% in the `cli` repo you own.** That's real, shippable work, and it's the correct first step even if you *did* have the backend.

The middle row is the interesting one you might not have considered: because you own **`git-sync`**, you can build a **central review-on-mirror** flow — a CI job (GitHub Action / cron) that runs `git-sync` to mirror refs and runs `entire review` on the incoming changes, in one place, with one API key. That gets you *"everyone's pushes get reviewed centrally"* — the enticing property — **without** needing the hosted git server. It's not baked into the remote, but it's centralized and it's achievable with exactly the repos you have.

**What you genuinely *cannot* do with these repos:** the hosted "native fusion that serves blame/replay" and the **web UI** — those need `entire-core`/`entiredb`/`entire.io`, which you don't have access to. If the "beat GitHub" bet ultimately means a web surface, you'll need those repos or someone who owns them.

Let me record this repo-availability verdict so we don't re-derive it, then I'd suggest we scope the two client-side builds plus the git-sync CI variant.

# git-sync: Complete Feature Enumeration

## CLI Commands & Subcommands

1. **`git-sync sync`** — mirrors source refs into target (auto-bootstraps empty targets)
2. **`git-sync replicate`** — overwrites target refs to match source via relay only; fails rather than materializing locally
3. **`git-sync plan`** — previews sync actions without pushing; accepts same flags as `sync` and `--mode replicate`
4. **`git-sync convert-sha256`** — one-off SHA1 → SHA256 repo conversion from HTTP source to disk-based bare repo

## Flags & Options

The documentation references these categories but doesn't exhaustively list all flags in the provided excerpt:

- **Source/Target endpoints** — `--source-token`, `--target-token` (authentication)
- **Behavior modes** — `--mode replicate` (for planning replicate runs)
- **Filtering & mapping** — branch filtering, ref mapping, tag handling (detailed in docs/usage.md)
- **Safety controls** — `--force` (force updates), `--prune` (delete managed refs)
- **Performance bounds** — `--materialized-max-objects` (limits in-memory object count on fallback path)
- **Protocol selection** — configurable protocol flags (docs/usage.md)
- **SHA256 conversion specifics** — commit-message hash rewrites, origin-notes ref, sidecar mapping file

## Core Features & Capabilities

### Transfer Paths

**Relay Mode:** Streams source packs directly into target `receive-pack` without local object materialization. Memory remains bounded regardless of repo size. Used automatically when target supports relay.

**Materialized Fallback:** Fetches needed objects into in-memory `go-git` store when relay unavailable. Guarded by explicit object-count limit. Enables batching for large initial syncs.

### Protocol & Communication

- Smart HTTP with `info/refs` ref advertisement
- `upload-pack` fetch with target tip hashes advertised as `have`
- `receive-pack` push with explicit ref updates and streamed packfiles
- SSH support via local `ssh` binary (`ssh://`, SCP-style, `git+ssh://`)
- Fallback to `git-remote-<scheme>` helpers for custom schemes (e.g., `entire://`)

### Ref Operations

Creates, updates, force-updates, and deletes managed refs. Supports complete Git object history transfer (not shallow). Planning includes ref-only round-trips and optional `filter tree:0` ancestry checks.

### Authentication & Transport Injection

Token-based auth via flags. Library API supports custom auth and HTTP injection.

### Output

"emits typed JSON for automation" — structured results for each operation.

## Library vs CLI Usage

**CLI:** Standalone tool for remote-to-remote mirroring via command-line invocation.

**Library:** Go module at `entire.io/entire/git-sync`:
- **Stable API** (`Probe`, `Plan`, `Sync`, `Replicate`) — typed results, auth/HTTP injection
- **Unstable API** (`entire.io/entire/git-sync/unstable`) — advanced controls like `Bootstrap`, `Fetch`, batching knobs, heap measurement

## Limits & Constraints

- **Not bidirectional** — one-way only; reverse requires second invocation with swapped endpoints
- **Not a daemon** — one-shot operation; schedule via cron, CI, or event-driven worker
- **In-memory bounds** — materialized path scales with diff size; relay path memory is constant
- **No shallow sync** — transfers "complete Git object history required for selected refs"
- **Relay-dependent** — safe fast-forward updates use relay; non-relay-eligible ops (force, prune, deletes, tag retargets) require materialization

## Example Invocations

```bash
git-sync sync \
  --source-token "$GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN" \
  --target-token "$GITSYNC_TARGET_TOKEN" \
  https://github.com/source-org/source-repo.git \
  https://github.com/target-org/target-repo.git
```

Preview without pushing:
```bash
git-sync plan --source-token ... --target-token ... [repo URLs]
```

Force replication:
```bash
git-sync replicate --source-token ... --target-token ... [repo URLs]
```

## Installation Methods

- Homebrew: `brew tap entireio/tap && brew install --cask git-sync`
- Go: `go install entire.io/entire/git-sync/cmd/git-sync@latest` (requires Go 1.26+)
- From source: clone and `go build -o git-sync ./cmd/git-sync`

Here's the full picture of what `git-sync` actually does.

## What it is
A one-shot **CLI + Go library** that mirrors git refs from a **source remote to a target remote directly, remote-to-remote, with no local checkout**. It streams packfiles over Smart HTTP and keeps almost nothing on disk. It's a *tool you invoke* (cron/CI/worker), not a running server.

## Commands
- **`sync`** — mirror source refs into target; auto-bootstraps an empty target.
- **`replicate`** — force the target to exactly match source, **relay-only** (refuses to materialize locally — fails instead).
- **`plan`** — dry-run preview of what would change, no push. Takes the same flags as `sync`.
- **`convert-sha256`** — one-off SHA1→SHA256 repo conversion (rewrites commit hashes, writes a sidecar mapping + origin-notes ref).

## How it moves data (the clever part)
- **Relay mode (default when possible):** streams source packs straight into the target's `receive-pack`. **Memory stays constant regardless of repo size** — it never builds the object graph locally.
- **Materialized fallback:** when relay isn't possible (force-updates, prunes, deletes, tag retargets), it fetches objects into an in-memory `go-git` store, bounded by `--materialized-max-objects`.

## Capabilities
- Full-history transfer (not shallow); create/update/**force**-update/**delete** refs; **prune** managed refs.
- Branch/ref **filtering and mapping**, tag handling.
- Protocols: **Smart HTTP**, **SSH** (via the local `ssh` binary), and — notably — **falls back to `git-remote-<scheme>` helpers for custom schemes like `entire://`**. So it can talk to an Entire mirror.
- Token auth (`--source-token`/`--target-token`); the library lets you inject custom auth/HTTP.
- **Emits typed JSON** for automation — easy to script around.
- Usable as a Go library (`Probe`, `Plan`, `Sync`, `Replicate`, plus an `unstable` package with `Bootstrap`/`Fetch`/batching knobs).

## What it does *not* do
- **Not a server** — serves no endpoints; nothing pushes *to* it.
- **No hooks / interception** — no callback when refs pass through. (This is why it can't host a server-side review gate.)
- **One-way** — reverse sync = a second invocation with endpoints swapped.
- **Not a daemon** — you schedule it.

## What this means for our plan
git-sync is essentially **programmable mirroring glue**. It can't *be* the review gate, but it's the perfect engine for the **"central review-on-mirror in CI"** idea: a scheduled/triggered job does `git-sync sync GitHub → entire://mirror` (or the reverse), you run `entire review` on the changed refs, act on the JSON, and the sync is memory-cheap even for huge repos. Its `plan` command even gives you the exact ref delta to feed the reviewer, and the Go library means you could build a small purpose-made binary around it rather than shelling out.

So: it's a strong building block for a *centralized* flow you control — just not a place to embed always-on server logic. Want me to sketch what that CI "sync-then-review" job would concretely look like using `plan` + `entire review`?

Entire's whole bet is: **capture the *why* (agent sessions, prompts, decisions) alongside the *what* (code), and let that context flow forward through the lifecycle.** Map it to the SDLC:

| Stage | Does context flow here yet? |
|---|---|

The gap that screams "next step" is **Review**. They've *captured* the intent, and they *have* a reviewer — but the two don't talk. The inevitable move is to **feed the captured context into the review.**

## The build: intent-aware review

> **GitHub reviews your diff. Entire reviews whether your diff did what you actually asked for.**

Instead of "here's a diff, find bugs," the reviewer gets the *session intent* too — the prompt, the constraints, the decisions from the checkpoints that produced the change — and evaluates against it:
- Did the agent actually do what was asked, or drift?
- Did it add anything *outside* the stated intent (scope creep, sneaky changes)?
- Does it honor the constraints the human gave ("use table-driven tests," "don't touch the auth layer")?

That's a review only Entire *can* do, because it's the only one that saw the intent. It's the cleanest one-sentence proof that you understand the product.

Sure — here's the idea in full.

## The problem it solves

When an agent (or a new human) starts working in a codebase, it sees the **code** but not the **reasoning**. So it re-derives context from scratch, and — worse — it *undoes deliberate decisions* because nothing told it they were deliberate. Classic case: an agent "cleans up" a weird-looking rate limit set to 100 req/s, not knowing a past session set it there on purpose because of a downstream quota. GitHub blame says "commit abc by Sarah" — useless. The *why* is gone.

Entire is the one system that captured that why (in the checkpoints/sessions). Today it's mostly readable by *humans* after the fact (`entire why`, `explain`, `search`). The next step: **make it readable by the *next agent*, live, mid-task.**

## What it is

An **MCP server** — Model Context Protocol, the standard way agents call out to external tools/context — that exposes Entire's captured provenance as tools any agent can call *while it works*. Before an agent edits code, it can ask:

- **`why_does_this_exist(file, line)`** → the prompt / session / decision that produced it (backed by `why`/`blame`/checkpoints)
- **`past_work_on(path)`** → prior sessions that touched this file, what was tried, what was rejected
- **`search_context(query)`** → semantic search over past sessions (backed by `search`/`pgr`-style ranking)
- **`intent_of(commit_or_branch)`** → the original ask behind a change

So the agent's own loop becomes: *"I'm about to change the rate limiter → call `why_does_this_exist` → oh, it's intentional, discussed in session Y → leave it / ask the human."* The context flows **into the next agent's plan/code stage automatically.**

## Why it fits their arc

It closes Entire's loop. Right now context flows *in* (capture) but only trickles back out to humans. This makes it flow *back into the work* — every agent that touches the repo gets smarter because of every agent that came before. That's the literal payoff of "capture the why": it's only worth capturing if it *feeds the next iteration*.

And it's **agent-agnostic** — any MCP-host agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, etc.) gets it for free, which is exactly Entire's "works with everyone" positioning. GitHub structurally can't ship this; it never captured the why.

## Why it's buildable with your repos

- Entire **already ships an MCP server** (`entire mcp`, the hidden stdio server) — you're extending an existing surface, not inventing one.
- The provenance primitives exist client-side: `why`, `blame`, `checkpoint explain`, `search`, and the checkpoint store (`cli-checkpoints`).
- **`pgr`** (their experimental MCP code-search server) is a working reference for the MCP-server shape and ranking/output-shaping.

So it's: take data Entire already has → expose it as MCP tools → done. No backend, no hosted inference.

## Intent-review vs. this one — how to choose

They're two ends of the same loop:

| | Intent-aware review | Provenance MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Lifecycle stage | Review (context flows *out* to catch drift) | Plan/Code of the *next* task (context flows *back in*) |
| Pitch | "reviews if you did what you asked" | "the next agent inherits why the code is the way it is" |
| Demo feel | one sharp command, easy to show live | infrastructure — needs an agent session to shine |
| Reuses | `entire review` + `--prompt` | `entire mcp` + `why`/`search` + `pgr` shape |

**Intent-review is the better *demo*** (crisp, self-contained, shows live). **Provenance MCP is the more *architecturally impressive*** — it shows you understand that captured context is only valuable if it re-enters the loop, and it's the thing that makes Entire compounding rather than just a recorder.

If the goal is "show them I see the vision," Provenance MCP arguably lands harder — it *is* the vision (context compounding across agents). If the goal is "ship something clean and legible in a demo," intent-review wins.

Yeah, I've been sloppy and mixed two different things together. Let me untangle it, because the confusion is fair.

There are **two separate questions** I kept blurring:
- **How** does the agent get the capability? (a command, a *skill*, an MCP tool, a *hook*) — this is just plumbing.
- **What** does the capability actually do? — this is the value.

**Existing Entire skills already cover one job: *retrieval*.** "Agent, go fetch the past context (why this exists, past work) so you can use it." That box is checked. The agent asks, it gets context, done.

My "two things" are **different jobs**, not different plumbing. Here they are, plainly:

### Thing 1 — Intent review: *judge the work against what you asked*
Not "fetch context." It takes **what you asked for** (the prompt/intent Entire captured) and **what the code actually did** (the diff), and tells you where they don't match.

> You told the agent: *"add caching to the user endpoint, don't touch auth."* It adds caching — and quietly also changes a token-expiry check in `auth/token.go`. A normal review (and GitHub) sees the diff, shrugs, says "looks fine." **Intent review says: "⚠️ you said don't touch auth — this diff modifies `auth/token.go:88`."**

That's a **verdict**, not a lookup. No existing skill does this, because skills *fetch* context — they don't *evaluate your work against it*. Value: catches silent drift, scope-creep, and violated constraints that are invisible to anyone who never saw the ask.

### Thing 2 — Context hook: *the same context, but forced in so the agent can't skip it*
Same kind of info a skill would fetch — but delivered by a **hook** that fires **automatically**, right before the agent edits a file, instead of waiting for the agent to *choose* to look.

> Agent opens `ratelimiter.go` to "simplify it." Before it touches anything, the hook injects: *"⚠️ the 100 req/s here was set deliberately in session #234 because of a downstream quota — don't raise it."* The agent never asked. It got told anyway.

Value: agents routinely **don't** check history, then undo intentional decisions. A skill is *opt-in* — help that's there **if the agent remembers**. A hook is *guaranteed* — it can't be ignored.

### The one thing that makes each different from existing skills

| | Existing skills | Thing 1: Intent review | Thing 2: Context hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| **When it runs** | when the agent decides to | after a change, as a check | automatically, before an edit |
| **What it does** | fetches past context | compares diff vs. your ask, flags gaps | pushes relevant decisions into view |
| **Can the agent skip it?** | **yes** (opt-in) | no — it's its own step | **no** — fires on its own |
| **New?** | already shipped | new **job** (judgment) | new **delivery** (enforced) |

So:
- **Skills = "context is *available* if the agent asks."**
- **Thing 1 = "we *check* whether you did what you asked."** ← new value: a verdict.
- **Thing 2 = "context is *unavoidable*, whether the agent asks or not."** ← new value: enforcement.

Honest read: **Thing 1 is the stronger of the two** — it does something genuinely new (evaluation), and it has the crispest demo. Thing 2's only novelty is *reliability* (same data, but can't be skipped), which matters only if agents skipping the opt-in path is a real problem in practice.

Honest answer: **mostly yes — and it's done at two levels, one of which isn't even Entire.**

**Level 1 — without Entire, agents already do this.** When you ask a modern agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) to build feature N, it *reads the existing codebase first* and mirrors the patterns it finds — the auth setup, the test style, how the last similar handler was written. Cursor/Copilot codebase indexing and semantic search make it sharper. **The code itself is the context**, and reading-before-writing is default behavior. So "don't start from scratch, follow how we did it before" is largely table stakes now.

**Level 2 — with Entire, the deeper version is *also* mostly built.** Entire's angle would be reusing not just the *code* but the *reasoning* behind past features — what was asked, what was tried, what was rejected. But that's exactly what they already ship:
- **`entire search`** — semantic + keyword search over past *sessions/checkpoints* ("how did we approach X before").
- **`entire-sem`** (a plugin you have) — *"entity-level semantic checkpoint context."*
- **`skills`** — literally *"search past work, explain code."*

So the agent can already pull "here's how similar features were built, and the intent behind them." This idea is in the **same family as provenance-MCP and intent-review** — *retrieval of past context* — which turns out to be a crowded, solved space (agents do it natively; Entire does it deeper three different ways).

**The one sliver that's less-built:** making it *proactive* — auto-surfacing "we built something very similar in feature 12, here's how" *when you start*, instead of waiting for the agent to search. But that's the "context hook" idea from earlier, whose only novelty is enforcement, not capability — marginal.

**The pattern worth internalizing (a filter for your own ideas):**

> **Retrieval of past context = solved and crowded.** The unbuilt value is in **actions and loops**, not more ways to fetch context.

Every "give the agent context" idea keeps colliding with something shipped, because context *access* is done. The stuff that's genuinely missing is where context drives an **action** — the ticket→agent→review→ticket loop we just landed on, where captured context becomes a *completed task*, not a search result.

Which is why I'd keep the momentum on **`entire-linear`** — it's still the one thing we've found that's actually unbuilt *and* high-value. Want me to scope that MVP, or do you want to keep pressure-testing ideas first?

You said think deeply, so let me start with your last question, because it reframes the other three: **"does this even make sense for Entire, or is it a general agent thing?"** That instinct is the sharpest thing you've said, and here's the honest answer:

## The loop is generic. The edges are Entire's.

"Agent grabs a ticket, works until done, opens a PR, keeps going" — that is **rapidly becoming a commodity.** GitHub Coding Agent, Devin, Cursor background agents, Copilot, Factory — they *all* do issue→PR autonomy. If Entire builds "another autonomous ticket-completing agent," it's a me-too with no moat, fighting better-funded orchestrators on their turf. So **don't build the middle of the loop.**

But think about what happens as the *act of coding* gets commoditized: the value doesn't disappear, it **moves to the two edges of the loop**:

- **Going in:** did the agent get the task *right*? Does it have the institutional context — how similar features were built, what was tried, what's off-limits?
- **Coming out:** can you *trust* the result? Was it reviewed against what was actually asked? Can you trace every change back to the intent?

**Entire already owns both edges.** It captured the context (the "in" edge) and it does intent-aware review + provenance (the "out" edge). The commoditizing middle — the agent typing code — is the one part Entire *shouldn't* try to own.

So the product statement that makes this "make sense for Entire":

> Entire isn't the agent that does your tickets. Entire is the layer that makes **any** agent's ticket-work **context-rich going in and intent-verified + traceable coming out.**

That's defensible, because the moat is the accumulated context + provenance graph — which compounds and which no generic orchestrator has. The loop isn't defensible; the edges are.

Now your three concrete questions, through that lens:

## 1. Add the ticket to the PR as context — how hard? Today?

**Trivially, today** — but be careful *which* version you build:

- **The dumb version** (paste ticket text into the PR body): an afternoon with one Linear GraphQL / Jira REST call + `gh pr edit`. But it's **not differentiated** — and Linear's native GitHub integration *already* auto-links PRs to issues. So this version adds ~nothing.
- **The Entire version** (barely more work): fetch the ticket → make it the **captured session intent / the review yardstick**, so `entire review` (which already reviews against intent) checks "did this PR do what the ticket asked," and provenance links each change → ticket. Same one API call, but now it feeds the *edges* that are Entire's. **This** is worth building.

Same effort, completely different value. Build the second.

## 2. Entire's own format / create tickets through Entire?

Split this into two, because one's smart and one's a trap:

- ✅ **A normalization layer — yes, do this.** Define a canonical `Task { title, intent, acceptance-criteria, links }`, with **pluggable fetchers** (`linear`, `jira`, `github`) that map any tracker into it. Then review, the agent, and provenance all speak *Task*, not *Linear ticket*. This is exactly the plugin/external-command pattern they already have, and it's what makes it "whatever tracker." This is the right architecture.
- ⚠️ **Entire as a tracker you create tickets in — no.** That's scope creep into Linear/Jira's job, where Entire has zero advantage. Nobody wants a fourth tracker.
- 💡 **But the *inverse* is very Entire:** create tickets **from captured context** — the agent finishes, and from what it *discovered mid-session* (a TODO, a latent bug, a follow-up) Entire files a Linear ticket automatically. That's context→ticket, which only Entire can do well because only Entire captured the session. Park it as a phase-2, but it's the differentiated direction, not "be a tracker."

## 3. Agent grabs it and keeps going?

Buildable (medium effort — it's the greenfield queue). But this **is** the generic/risky middle from question 4, and "keeps going" unattended is where reliability and trust break. My honest steer: **keep the human gate, lean on intent-review as the trust checkpoint.** Ship "one ticket, end-to-end, human approves the merge" first. The continuous unattended version is a demo-risk *and* the least differentiated thing you could build.

---

**Net:** the idea makes total sense for Entire — *if* Entire plays the context+trust layer on the loop, not the agent in it. The `entire-linear` MVP I'd scope is exactly the edges: **ticket → (normalized Task) → agent works with Entire's institutional context → `entire review` verifies against the ticket → PR carries the ticket link + provenance + verdict → human approves.** Small, mostly reuse, and every piece plays to something only Entire has.

Confirmed — and it's cleaner than I expected. Every major tracker exposes the exact four primitives your loop needs (**auth → fetch → comment → update status**), plus native GitHub PR↔issue linking. Here's the map:

| Tracker | Auth (MVP) | Fetch ticket | Comment back | Update status | Native GitHub PR link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Linear** | API key (or OAuth) | GraphQL query | `commentCreate` | `issueUpdate` + `stateId` | ✅ magic-word / branch, auto-status |
| **Jira Cloud** | API token (basic) / OAuth 3LO | GET issue (REST v3) | POST comment | Transition endpoint (+comment) | ✅ smart commits / PR linking |
| **Azure DevOps** | PAT | Work Items REST | comment API | work-item update | ✅ `#`/`!` mentions, link from item |
| **ClickUp** | API token | public API | task comment | task update | ✅ commit/branch/PR links + automations |
| **Asana / Shortcut** | token | GET task/story | stories/comment | update workflow state | ✅ GitHub integrations |
| **GitHub Issues** | already via `gh` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | native |

So: **yes, fully possible today**, and with just an API token per tracker for the MVP (no OAuth dance required to start).

Three things worth pulling out of this:

**1. Your normalization-layer instinct is validated by reality.** Every tracker offers the *same* operations, so the canonical `Task` + pluggable-fetcher design isn't just clean — it maps 1:1 to what each API already gives you. Each adapter is roughly an afternoon.

**2. Linear went further — it has *first-class agent rails.*** Beyond the plain API, Linear ships an **Agents API** with `actor=app` OAuth (tokens that act *as the app*, not a user) and agent webhooks. That means Entire can appear in Linear **as a real agent** — assigned tickets, responding in-thread — not just a script polling. Linear built the plumbing for exactly this; it's the deepest integration and it *lowers* your effort. Start Linear-first for this reason alone. ([Linear Agents docs](https://linear.app/developers/agents), [demo](https://github.com/linear/linear-agent-demo))

**3. It reinforces "don't build the dumb version."** All of them *already* auto-link PRs to tickets natively (Linear/Jira/ADO/ClickUp). So "attach the ticket to the PR" is a solved commodity — the trackers do it themselves. Your build is the **Entire edges**: ticket-as-captured-intent going in, `entire review` verdict + provenance coming out. That's the part none of these platforms do.

# Building a Linear Agent: Registration, Delegation, and Interaction

## 1. Agent Registration and Installation

Agents are registered via OAuth2 with a special parameter. To install as an app rather than a user, "add the `actor=app` parameter to switch to an app installation rather than requesting authentication" in the OAuth authorization URL. This requires workspace admin permissions.

**Key scopes to request:**
- `app:assignable` – enables assignment as issue delegate
- `app:mentionable` – allows @mentions in issues/documents
- `customer:read/write` and `initiative:read/write` – for accessing those entity types

Each workspace installation grants your app "a _unique ID for each workspace_" retrievable via the GraphQL `viewer.id` query. Store this ID with your access token for workspace identification.

## 2. Delegating Work to an Agent

Work flows to agents through three channels:

1. **Issue Assignment** – Users assign issues directly; the agent becomes the `delegate` (not assignee, preserving human ownership)
2. **@mentions** – Users mention the agent in comments/documents
3. **Automatic Sessions** – "Sessions are created automatically when an agent is mentioned or delegated an issue"

**Webhook fired:** When delegated, a `created` AgentSessionEvent webhook delivers the `agentSession` object containing the issue, comments, and context.

## 3. Agent Session Concept and Lifecycle

An Agent Session tracks one task's complete lifecycle. "Session state is visible to users, and updated automatically based on the agent's emitted activities. No manual state management is required."

**Lifecycle:**
- Session created when issue is assigned or agent is mentioned
- Agent should "Emit a `thought` activity within 10 seconds to acknowledge the session has begun"
- Agent posts progress updates via Agent Activities
- Session concludes when work completes

## 4. Posting Updates: Agent Activities

Agents respond by emitting **Agent Activities** which automatically update visible session state. The agent should:

- Use the `promptContext` field to "construct a formatted string containing the session's relevant context, such as issue details, comments, and guidance"
- Post `thought` activities to signal acknowledgment
- Create comments and update issues via API mutations
- Emit activities that drive session state transitions

## 5. Built-in UI Affordances

The document doesn't detail specific emoji, status icons, or visual indicators. It confirms that "Session state is visible to users," implying Linear renders session progress automatically—but concrete UI components aren't documented in this preview material.

---

**Key Webhook Types:** `AgentSessionEvent` (created), `PermissionChange`

**Key Mutations:** Issue assignment, comment creation, activity emission (specific mutation names not detailed in preview docs)

content.text:
Pulled Linear's agent model, and it's better than I hoped — it changes the ambition ceiling. Here's the confirmation and the plan built on it.

## What Linear's agent rails give you

Linear has a **first-class Agent** concept, and it maps almost eerily well onto the "edges, not middle" design:

- **Registration:** OAuth with `actor=app` (workspace admin installs it) + scopes `app:assignable`, `app:mentionable`. Entire becomes a real app-actor, not a user script.
- **Delegation (3 ways):** assign an issue to Entire (it becomes **delegate**, the human keeps ownership), @mention it, or auto-session. A `AgentSessionEvent(created)` webhook fires with the issue + context.
- **Agent Session:** tracks one task's whole lifecycle, and **its state is rendered to users by Linear automatically** from the activities you emit. You emit a `thought` within 10s to ack, then stream progress, then complete.
- **`promptContext` field:** a purpose-built slot for "the session's relevant context — issue details, comments, guidance."

## The unlock this creates

**Linear's Agent Session UI is the live progress-and-context surface we said was blocked** (it needed `entire.io`, which you don't have). You get it *for free, inside Linear*: as Entire's agent works, its `thought`/progress activities render as a live session; the `entire review` verdict posts as the closing activity. And `promptContext` is a literal, designed home for Entire's **context-in edge** — you inject the institutional context (how past features were built) right there.

So the two edges land exactly on Linear primitives:

| Entire edge | Linear primitive |
|---|---|
| **Context-in** (institutional memory) | inject into `promptContext` on session start |
| agent does the work (the generic middle) | your `LaunchFixAgent`, checkpoints capture |
| live progress / provenance surfacing | emit **Agent Activities** → native session UI |
| **Trust-out** (intent-review verdict) | closing activity + comment; PR auto-linked via Linear's native GitHub integration |

You are the edges; Linear renders the middle. No custom UI, no `entire.io` needed.

## Honest build phases

**Phase 1 — polling MVP (pure plugin, zero infra):** `entire linear take <id>` (or poll issues delegated to you) → fetch via GraphQL → `LaunchFixAgent` with context → `entire review` (ticket = intent) → post verdict comment + move state. This proves the whole loop client-side, no server. An afternoon per piece.

**Phase 2 — agent-native (the "full advantage" version):** register `actor=app`, receive `AgentSessionEvent`, emit activities → the live Linear session experience. **One honest wrinkle:** webhooks need an inbound HTTP endpoint, which a pure CLI plugin doesn't have. Two ways around it: (a) a tiny hosted webhook receiver, or (b) *approximate* it by polling for delegated issues and still emitting agent activities via the API — most of the magic (session UI, context injection, verdict) without hosting. Real-time push is the only thing that truly needs the endpoint.

## The one decision for later

Phase 2's real-time version needs somewhere to receive webhooks. So: **can you stand up a tiny always-on endpoint** (even a serverless function), or should we stay pure-CLI and drive agent sessions by polling? That's the only fork — and it doesn't block Phase 1 at all.

My recommendation: **build Phase 1 now** (it's the whole loop, no infra, immediately dogfoodable by the Linear-native Entire team), designed so the same `Task` adapter + review wiring slot straight into Phase 2.

Want me to scaffold the `entire-linear` plugin now — repo skeleton on the `roger-roger`/`entire-run` pattern, the `Task` type + Linear GraphQL fetcher, and the `LaunchFixAgent` + `entire review` wiring for the Phase 1 loop?

Phase 1 is one command that turns a Linear ticket into a reviewed draft PR. No webhooks, no infra, no autonomy — you trigger it, a human approves the result. Here's the whole thing, concretely, with a sample ticket **ENG-142: "Add rate limiting to the /export endpoint."**

**You run:** `entire linear take ENG-142` (or it lists your assigned tickets and you pick one).

Then it does, in order:

1. **Fetch the ticket** — one Linear GraphQL call by ID → pulls title, description, acceptance criteria, comments, labels. *(new — small)*
2. **Normalize it** into a canonical `Task { title, intent, acceptance, links }`, so the rest is tracker-agnostic. *(new — small)*
3. **Gather context — the Entire edge.** Use `entire search` / checkpoints / `entire-sem` to pull *how similar things were built here* — e.g. "we added rate limiting to `/report` in session #88, here's the pattern and the 100 req/s decision." This is the part that makes it Entire and not a generic script. *(reuse + light glue)*
4. **Launch the agent on it** — `LaunchFixAgent` spawns your coding agent (Claude Code, etc.) with the prompt = **ticket + that gathered context**. The agent writes the code, runs tests, commits on a branch. Entire's hooks **checkpoint the whole session automatically** (full capture, provenance). *(reuse)*
5. **Review against the ticket — the other Entire edge.** Run `entire review`, which already reviews a diff against captured intent — here **the ticket is the intent**. Verdict: *did it actually do what ENG-142 asked? any scope-creep / drift?* (e.g. "⚠️ also modified `auth/token.go`, not in scope"). *(reuse)*
6. **PR gets linked** — the branch/PR is created; Linear's **native GitHub integration** auto-links PR ↔ ENG-142 via the branch name. *(reuse — Linear does it)*
7. **Report back to Linear** — post a comment on ENG-142: what was done, the PR link, the review verdict; move the ticket to **"In Review."** *(new — small Linear mutations)*
8. **You approve** — you read the PR + the verdict, merge. Linear's GitHub automation flips ENG-142 to **Done.** *(human gate — deliberate)*

**End to end:** `entire linear take ENG-142` → a branch/PR that was built *with* your codebase's institutional context and *checked* against the ticket, with the summary + verdict posted back on the ticket — waiting for your approval.

**What Phase 1 does NOT do (on purpose):**
- No live Linear "agent session" UI (that's Phase 2 / `actor=app` + webhooks).
- No queue / "keep going" across tickets (that's the generic autonomous middle — deliberately last).
- No unattended merge — a human always approves.

**Reuse vs. new:** steps 3–6 are almost entirely existing Entire machinery; the only genuinely new code is *fetch ticket* (1–2) and *post back + status* (7) — both small Linear API calls. That's why it's a few days, not a rewrite.

The whole point of Phase 1: prove the **edges** (context-in, trust-out) on a real ticket, with the smallest possible new surface. Want me to scaffold it?

Good instinct — and it actually improves the design. Let me answer the "best way" honestly, because I don't think baking the link into `take` is right once you add the "link anytime" requirement.

## Separate *link* from *take*

The retroactive requirement is telling you these are two different operations that `take` was conflating:

- **link** = attach a ticket to the current work (branch/session). Pure metadata. Idempotent. Works before, during, or after.
- **take** = link *and* launch an agent from scratch.

So **`link` is the primitive**, and `take` is just `link + launch`. Everything else (review-against-ticket, post-back, context injection) keys off the link, not off how you started.

## The best way to link (my opinion)

Not one command — a **combo that makes it "just work":**

1. **Auto-detect from the branch name.** Linear's "copy git branch" gives you `you/eng-142-add-rate-limiting`, and its GitHub integration already links via that. So if your branch encodes the ticket, Entire **infers the link with zero commands.** Most of the time you do nothing.
2. **Explicit `entire linear link ENG-142`** as the fallback — for when the branch name doesn't encode it, or you started on a random branch and forgot. Anytime, idempotent, re-runnable.

That combo means it's *automatic when possible, always recoverable when not* — which is exactly your "if you forgot, it still works."

**One correctness note on your syntax:** `-ticket` (single dash) breaks in cobra/pflag — it reads as stacked short flags `-t -i -c…`. Use a **positional** (`entire linear link ENG-142`) or a **double-dash flag** (`--ticket ENG-142`, with `-t` as the shorthand). Positional reads best for the primary arg.

## Why "link later" genuinely just works

Here's the elegant part — it falls straight out of what Entire *already is*. Entire **passively captures every session continuously** via hooks, whether or not a ticket is linked. So when you link late, **the context is already recorded** — you're not recovering anything, you're just giving already-captured work a home. Concretely, `link` writes the ticket ID into Entire's branch/session state; everything downstream reads it:

- **Link before you start** → agent + review use it going forward.
- **Link mid-work** → the sessions/checkpoints already on this branch get associated; review + post-back use it from here.
- **Link after you're done** (forgot until PR time) → `entire linear link ENG-142` → `entire review` reviews the *existing* diff against the ticket, posts the summary + verdict back. Full value, zero lost work.

That last case is the one you care about, and it works precisely *because* Entire was recording the whole time. Late linking is a first-class path, not a bolt-on.

## How the pieces compose

- `entire linear link ENG-142` — attach ticket to current branch/session (or auto-inferred from branch name).
- `entire review` — if a ticket is linked, it *automatically* uses it as the intent yardstick. No extra args.
- On commit/PR — post summary + verdict back to the linked ticket, move it to "In Review."
- `entire linear take ENG-142` — convenience = link + `LaunchFixAgent` for the from-scratch flow.
- `entire linear status` / `unlink` — inspect or clear.

So Phase 1 becomes: **link (however — auto or manual, anytime) → work (agent or you) → review-against-ticket → post back → approve.** The linking is decoupled, so it survives you forgetting.

Want me to fold this into the scaffold — `link` as the core command with branch auto-detection, `take` as link+launch, and the linked-ticket state that `review` and post-back read from?

Yes — this makes total sense, and it's *more* right than `linear`, for two reasons:

1. **It matches Entire's own conventions exactly.** Entire is built around noun groups with verb children (`session`, `checkpoint`, `agent`…), with files named `<noun>_group.go` / `<noun>_<verb>.go`. `entire ticket` as a new noun group drops right in — it'll feel native, not bolted-on.
2. **It's the normalization layer made visible.** We said the smart architecture is a canonical `Task` + pluggable fetchers. Naming the command `ticket` (not `linear`) *is* that boundary: the command surface is provider-agnostic; only the provider behind `setup` changes. Linear today, Jira/GitHub/etc. later, **zero command changes.**

## Standard syntax

```
entire ticket                     # bare: show this branch's linked ticket + platform status (+ --json)
entire ticket setup               # choose platform + credentials (interactive; Linear only for now)
entire ticket link [ID]           # link a ticket to the current branch/session
entire ticket unlink              # remove the link from the current branch/session
entire ticket start [ID]          # link + launch an agent to work it from scratch
entire ticket status [--json]     # what's linked here + whether the platform is configured
```

Flags, following how `review`/`configure` already work:
- **`setup`** — interactive `huh` form (accessible-mode aware): pick platform → enter token → pick team/workspace. Non-interactive: `--platform linear --token <t> --team <id>`.
- **`link [ID]`** — ID optional: **omit it and Entire auto-detects from the branch name** (Linear's `you/eng-142-…` format). `--force` to overwrite an existing link.
- **`start [ID]`** — reuses launch flags: `--agent`, `--model`, `--no-review`.
- IDs are **opaque to the CLI** — `ENG-142` (Linear), `PROJ-123` (Jira), `#123` (GitHub) all just get handed to the active provider to parse. That's what keeps it agnostic.

## A day in the life

```
entire ticket setup                 # once: pick Linear, paste API key, choose team
entire ticket start ENG-142         # from-scratch: link + agent works it + review + posts back
# — or, you already coded something and forgot —
git switch fix/export-throttle
entire ticket link ENG-142          # link late; your captured work is already there
entire review                       # auto-uses ENG-142 as the intent; posts verdict back
```

## Under the hood (the agnostic core)

```go
type Provider interface {
    Name() string
    Fetch(ctx, id) (Task, error)          // → canonical Task{Title, Intent, Acceptance, Links}
    Comment(ctx, id, body) error
    SetState(ctx, id, state) error
    ResolveFromBranch(branch) (id, ok)    // auto-detect
}
```
`ticket.platform` (in settings) selects the provider; the **token lives in the token store / `settings.local.json`** (gitignored), never committed. `LinearProvider` implements it now; adding Jira later is just a new file that satisfies the interface — no command or Task changes.

So the three things you wanted map cleanly: **`setup`** (add the platform) → **`link`/`unlink`** (attach a ticket, anytime) → **`start`** (link + do it). And `review`/post-back read the link, so the "forgot to link" path works because Entire was capturing all along.

package ticket

import (
	"testing"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestLinkStore_RoundTrip(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	store := newLinkStoreWithDir(t.TempDir())

	_, ok, err := store.get("main")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.False(t, ok, "no link before any is set")

	require.NoError(t, store.set("feature/x", Link{Platform: "linear", ID: "ENG-1"}))
	got, ok, err := store.get("feature/x")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.True(t, ok)
	assert.Equal(t, "ENG-1", got.ID)
	assert.Equal(t, "linear", got.Platform)

	// A second branch does not disturb the first.
	require.NoError(t, store.set("feature/y", Link{Platform: "linear", ID: "ENG-2"}))
	got, ok, err = store.get("feature/x")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.True(t, ok)
	assert.Equal(t, "ENG-1", got.ID)

	removed, err := store.del("feature/x")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.True(t, removed)

	_, ok, err = store.get("feature/x")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.False(t, ok)

	// Deleting an absent branch reports false, not an error.
	removed, err = store.del("feature/x")
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.False(t, removed)
}

## The stack (base → top)

| # | Branch | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `feat/ticket-base` | `ticket` package: canonical `Task`/`State`, `Provider` interface, hidden `ticket` group on root |
| 2 | `feat/ticket-setup` | `settings.TicketConfig`, tokenstore creds, `huh` setup form + non-interactive flags |
| 3 | `feat/ticket-link` | per-branch link store (git common dir), `link`/`unlink`, `CurrentLink` |
| 4 | `feat/ticket-start` | `start` → `LaunchFix` via cli-package bridge (no import cycle), `Deps` |
| 5 | `feat/ticket-linear` | Linear GraphQL provider (`Fetch`/`Comment`/`SetState`/`ResolveFromBranch`), auto-detect in `link`, ticket-fetch in `start` |

**13 passing test cases**, and the command tree resolves: `entire ticket {setup,link,unlink,start}`.

## Conventions I matched (and gotchas I hit)
- Built it **natively** as a hidden-during-maturation noun group like `investigate`/`review` — not a plugin — since that's how the repo does maturing features.
- **`gochecknoinits`** → providers wire explicitly via the bridge, no `init()`. **`unparam`** → `Deps` only introduced when first used (PR4). **`huh` is `charm.land/huh/v2`**, not the github path. ## What's deliberately deferred (honest notes, in commit messages too)
- `start`'s agent gets the ticket as context, but the **review post-back loop** (Comment/SetState are implemented but not yet invoked) and the **Linear `actor=app` agent-session UI** are the next layer — the "trust-out edge" and Phase 2.

## 3. Real Linear (needs a token + a real ticket)

Get a personal API key from Linear: **Settings → Security & access → Personal API keys**. Your `--team` is the issue prefix (the `ENG` in `ENG-142`). Then:


**Heads-up on `start`:** it fetches the real ticket *and then launches `claude-code`* to work it — so it runs a real agent (real tokens/cost). That's the true end-to-end, but it's not a cheap "did the fetch work" check.

There's no cheap way to test the **real Linear `Fetch`** in isolation right now — it only runs as the first step of `start`, which launches an agent. The clean fix is a tiny **`--dry-run` / `--print-prompt` flag on `start`** that fetches the ticket, prints the composed prompt, and exits *without* launching the agent. That'd let you verify the real API round-trip (and see exactly what the agent would get) for free.

Here's the why: our `linearProvider` authenticates by putting the key straight into the `Authorization` header (no `Bearer` prefix) — `req.Header.Set("Authorization", p.token)`. That's exactly the **Personal API key** model. Get it from **Linear → Settings → Security & access → Personal API keys → New API key** (the key looks like `lin_api_…`; paste it raw into `--token`).

A personal key acts **as you**, so it can already do everything `setup`/`link`/`start` need for testing: read `ENG-142`, and later post comments / change status as your user.

What you *don't* want yet:
- **OAuth / `actor=app` (the "agent" token)** — this is the one that makes Entire show up in Linear *as its own agent* with the live Agent Session UI. That's the **Phase 2** integration we haven't built. It needs a registered OAuth app + the `actor=app` flow, and our current provider doesn't speak it. Skip it for now.

So: **Personal API key** for testing today; the app/agent token comes when we build the Agent Sessions layer.

Confirmed: the built binary has `ticket`; your shell just runs the installed release at `~/.local/bin/entire`. Two ways to fix that:

**Option A — install the branch build over your shell's `entire`** (so `entire ticket …` just works everywhere):
```bash
cp /tmp/entire ~/.local/bin/entire
```
It's a superset of your current build (same repo + the `ticket` work), and reversible — reinstall the release later to revert. After this, `entire ticket status` works in your shell.

**Option B — non-destructive**, just use the built binary directly:
```bash
/tmp/entire ticket status
```
or alias it: `alias edev=/tmp/entire`.

**Either way, one important thing:** `ticket` config and links are **per-repo**, so you have to run `setup` in the repo you want to use it in first. In a fresh repo:
```bash
cd /path/to/your/repo
entire ticket setup --platform linear --team MOH --token <fresh-key>   # token → your macOS keychain
entire ticket status
entire ticket start MOH-56          # links + launches an agent with the ticket
```
(Our earlier test lived in `/tmp/ticket-test` with a file-backed token store via env vars — that was just sandbox isolation. For real use, plain `setup` uses your keychain.)

Also note: `ticket` is `Hidden`, so it won't appear in `entire help` — that's intentional (matures like `review`/`investigate`), but every `entire ticket …` command runs.

Ah, I see the confusion — this is the key mental-model bit. Let me clear it up.

## Source code ≠ the installed command

`entire` (the command your shell runs) is a **pre-compiled binary** sitting at `~/.local/bin/entire`. It was built and installed at some point in the past and **frozen**. It does *not* read your source files when it runs.

Your branch (`feat/ticket-status`, checked out in `/Users/mohit/Desktop/cli`) has the new `ticket` code — but only as **source**. Editing/checking out source doesn't change that installed binary. So:

> You *are* on the right branch. The code *is* there. But typing `entire` runs the old compiled binary, not your source.

To run your branch's code, you have to **compile it**. That's the missing step — not the branch, not the tab.

## Testing it right now (three ways)

**1. Run your branch's source directly** (no install) — from the repo:
```bash
cd /Users/mohit/Desktop/cli        # already on feat/ticket-status
go run ./cmd/entire ticket status
```
`go run` compiles your current source and runs it. This *will* print "not configured" (the cli repo has no ticket setup) — but that itself proves the command now exists and runs from your branch.

**2. A new tab — but only if the binary has it.** Opening a new tab won't help by itself: a new tab has the same PATH → same old `~/.local/bin/entire` → still no `ticket`. A tab isn't the missing piece; compiling is.

**3. Make `entire` in any tab have it** — install the branch build over the installed one:
```bash
cp /tmp/entire ~/.local/bin/entire
```
After that, open a new tab and `entire ticket status` works like a normal command. Reversible: reinstall the release later to revert.

## To actually see it do something (any of the above)

`ticket` config/links are **per-repo**, so run setup in whatever repo you're testing in:
```bash
cd /some/git/repo
entire ticket setup --platform linear --team MOH --token <FRESH-key>
entire ticket status        # now shows config + the live MOH-56
```
